title: Logarithmic randomized online labeling
formal: Is there one uniform randomized online list-labeling algorithm and a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every capacity \(n\ge2\) and every obliviously fixed valid sequence of \(M\ge0\) insertions and deletions, its expected total movement cost is at most \[C\bigl(n+M\log_2(n+2)\bigr)?\] At most \(n\) items are live, and their order-preserving labels must lie in \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\). Cost, validity and the oblivious-adversary convention are defined below.
why: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.

sentences: Online labeling stores a changing ordered list in an array with spare slots.
An update can force existing items to change labels.
The question asks for logarithmic expected amortized movement with a constant fraction of spare space.
The adversary fixes the full update sequence independently of the random choices.
Local computation is free, so the target does not assert logarithmic machine running time.

definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update.

context_blocks.text: List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The selected target keeps constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary. It asks whether the known logarithmic lower-bound scale is achievable, without requesting the entire optimum if that endpoint fails.

answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.
